sources.title: Augustin-Jean Fresnel (Q187241), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-04): English label 'Augustin-Jean Fresnel', description 'French engineer and physicist (1788-1827)', Korean label 오귀스탱 장 프레넬, birth 10 May 1788 and death 14 July 1827, image the frontispiece of the 1866 Oeuvres completes. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Augustin-Jean Fresnel' (article body read from the public page) and the Britannica article 'Fresnel lens' (read). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: French physicist (1788-1827) who significantly contributed to optics and helped establish the wave theory of light that Thomas Young advanced; he began optics research in 1814 while working as an engineer building roads, his experiments with interference fringes and diffraction led him to the wave theory, in 1819 he presented his diffraction work to the French Academy of Sciences, where his model predicted a bright spot at the centre of a shadow, later observed and named Poisson's spot; he combined Young's interference principle with Huygens' construction; the Fresnel lens, which divides a lens into concentric rings to reduce weight, was adopted by him in 1821 for lighthouses (the idea of dividing a lens into rings having come from Buffon in 1748). Some dates in the Q&A-style summary of the biography page (for example the year of the transverse-wave conclusion) differ from MacTutor and were not used. Scholarly reference; its praise is retrospective.

MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews), 'Augustin Fresnel' by J. J. O'Connor and E. F. Robertson (full biography read, including its quotations from the Dictionary of Scientific Biography). Covers the engineering career, the start of his light experiments in 1814, the black-paper diffraction experiment, the 1815-16 papers, the two-mirror interference experiments, the 1819 Academy prize judged by a committee not well disposed to the wave theory (Poisson's bright spot, tested at Arago's request), the 1821 claim that light is a transverse wave which even Arago did not accept, double refraction, the Lighthouse Commission and compound lenses, election to the Academy in 1823 and the Rumford Medal in 1827, and the Dictionary of Scientific Biography's character summary (attentive to detail, systematic, thorough; tenacious in convictions; rankling self-righteousness at times). Scholarly history site; his political episodes, family and health are not used.

Francois Arago, biographical memoir of Fresnel (read at the Academy of Sciences in 1830), in the English translation by Baden Powell in 'Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men' (London, 1859; Internet Archive text; read: the early optical researches, the passage on never publishing without checking earlier work, the engineering duties, the lighthouse lenses and the concentric-wick lamp, the Cordouan light built in July 1823, the costs of his instruments, and the translator's notes quoting Fresnel's own acknowledgement of Young's priority and Whewell's account of the transverse-vibration memoir). Written by Fresnel's close friend and collaborator, so admiring; the memoir's political passages and the translator's long optical notes were not used.

Robert Moon, 'Fresnel and His Followers: A Criticism' (Cambridge, 1849; Internet Archive text; preface and contents read). A hostile 19th-century Cambridge mathematician who calls Fresnel's theory 'absurd', says its hypotheses were accepted with 'not a shadow of evidence' and condemns the whole system of investigation. COUNTER-VOICE on his method of theory-building; his critique concerns the physics, not Fresnel's conduct, and later physics did not follow it (the wave theory prevailed, as Britannica and MacTutor report). The body of the book was not read.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_fresnel_mactutor, src_fresnel_britannica, src_fresnel_arago, src_fresnel_moon | 1815-1819 | history site, encyclopedia, collaborator's memoir, hostile critic] MacTutor says he derived formulae for the positions of bright and dark diffraction lines from where vibrations were in phase and out of phase and, in 1819, calculated the intensity of light at every point behind the diffracting screen; Poisson, from Fresnel's mathematics, deduced the bright spot at the centre of a disk's shadow and Arago's test confirmed it (MacTutor, Britannica); Arago adds that he never published a memoir without checking with friends that he was not repeating earlier work. The one contrary voice, Moon (1849), calls Fresnel's assumptions unsupported, a view that later physics did not follow, but it shows the method was disputed. The Poisson prediction was made by Poisson and the praise is partly retrospective, so confidence is moderate. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): analytical_rigor lowered from 80 / 0.62 to 76 / 0.58 because concentrated in MacTutor, Britannica and Arago, an admiring collaborator, against one hostile critic.

experimentation.rationale: [src_fresnel_mactutor, src_fresnel_arago | 1814-1823 | history site, collaborator's memoir] MacTutor describes the experiment in which he attached black paper to one edge of a diffracting object, saw the bright bands inside the shadow vanish, and so deduced which bands came from one edge or both, and his two-mirror interference experiments that verified his calculated patterns; Arago records the joint polarisation experiments and the long series of experiments with a multiple-wick lamp for the lighthouse lenses, and says instruments took a considerable part of his income. Specific, repeated experimental work is reported by an independent history site and an admiring collaborator.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_fresnel_mactutor, src_fresnel_arago, src_fresnel_britannica, src_fresnel_moon | 1815-1821 | history site, collaborator's memoir, encyclopedia, hostile critic] MacTutor says his experiments convinced him of the wave theory when the corpuscular theory was almost universally held, that the Academy committee judging his 1819 entry was not well disposed to it, and that in 1821 he claimed with certainty that light is a transverse wave, a step too far for most, even Arago, before he deduced double refraction from it; a note in the Arago translation (citing Whewell) says Arago lacked the courage to publish the transverse-vibration idea, so that part of the memoir appeared under Fresnel's name alone. Britannica says he began unaware of Young's work. Moon's hostile 1849 critique shows the position remained contested. Several sources agree he held and published a minority position against consensus. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): independent_thinking lowered from 80 / 0.64 to 76 / 0.58 because the same concentration; the independence is read from outcome and from the collaborator memoir.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_fresnel_britannica, src_fresnel_mactutor, src_fresnel_arago | 1815-1823 | encyclopedia, history site, collaborator's memoir] Britannica says he combined Young's interference principle with Huygens' construction and calculated the intensity patterns of interfering secondary wavelets, and MacTutor that he moved beyond Young to a new mathematical formulation; the Fresnel lens, dividing a lens into concentric rings, was applied by him to lighthouses (Britannica, Arago), although Britannica credits the ring idea to Buffon in 1748 and Arago admits Condorcet and Buffon had earlier projects. Much of the original optics was done unaware of Young, Huygens and Euler, so the novelty lies in the synthesis and the engineering application, not in the first ideas; confidence moderate.

collaboration.rationale: [src_fresnel_mactutor, src_fresnel_arago | 1816-1823 | history site, collaborator's memoir] MacTutor says that he and Arago undertook further polarisation work together, which led to the discovery of circularly polarised light; Arago says the two devoted themselves jointly to the concentric-wick lamp for the lighthouse lens; a note in the translation quotes Fresnel's own words acknowledging that Young had published the transverse-vibration idea before him. The main account of the partnership comes from Arago himself and the acknowledgement is self-report, so the row is moderate.

persistence.rationale: [src_fresnel_mactutor, src_fresnel_arago | 1816-1823 | history site, collaborator's memoir] MacTutor says that once he was a working engineer he could research only in his vacations and kept requesting leave to go to Paris for his investigations, and quotes the Dictionary of Scientific Biography on the 'perseverance' he brought to the lighthouse work; Arago says the lens idea dated from about 1820 and was built at Cordouan in July 1823, and that experimental instruments absorbed a large part of his income. The record is of sustained effort across years alongside paid duties; the row deliberately does not rest on any reading of his health.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_fresnel_mactutor, src_fresnel_arago | 1819-1827 | history site quoting the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, collaborator's memoir] The Dictionary of Scientific Biography, as quoted by MacTutor, says he held to his convictions tenaciously, defended them with courage and vigour, voiced outrage when others fell short of his own ethical standards and at times approached 'rankling self-righteousness'; Arago says he showed sternness to anyone who submitted an ambiguous account in his engineering duties. These are retrospective characterisations by an encyclopedia entry and an admiring friend, without a specific dated confrontation in the sources read, hence low confidence; the political part of the quoted passage is not scored.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_fresnel_mactutor, src_fresnel_arago | 1815-1827 | history site quoting the Dictionary of Scientific Biography, collaborator's memoir] The Dictionary of Scientific Biography, quoted by MacTutor, calls him always attentive to detail, systematic and thorough, and Arago says he performed his engineering duties with rigorous scrupulousness, estimating contractors' work carefully, and became cautious about publishing until he had checked earlier literature. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed because it rests on a generic adjective trio paraphrasing an admiring eulogy; lowered from 72 / 0.52 to 68 / 0.46 because no specific incident of detailed work is cited beyond duties and publication habits.

portrait.source: Frontispiece engraving of Augustin Fresnel signed 'E. Rosotte sculp. d'apres A. Tardieu' in the official edition 'Oeuvres completes d'Augustin Fresnel', tome 1 (Paris: Imprimerie imperiale, 1866), in the Internet Archive copy digitised from the New York Public Library (page image 2500 x 3275). The engraving is a later print after a portrait by Ambroise Tardieu; none of the sources read documents a sitting, so it is not presented as a likeness. This file is the engraving only, cropped from the scan and downscaled to 1058 x 1200 with no upscaling.
